classification.difficultyReason: Explain how repeated sine values can hide a distinct polynomial root, contrasting this with cosine being one-to-one over the relevant angle interval.

content.prompt: Explain why a substitution like $x=\sin\theta$ to reduce a polynomial to $\sin3\theta=\frac12$ needs extra care, whereas $x=\cos\theta$ to reduce to $\cos3\theta=\frac12$ does not? What is it about the first substitution that makes it so much more tricky?

answer.short:
For increasing $\theta\ge0$, sine starts repeating values after $\theta=\frac\pi2$, while cosine is one-to-one on $[0,\pi]$. Sine may repeat values before all three distinct polynomial roots have been found.

Continue finding angles and discard repeated values of $x$.
answer.worked:
For increasing $\theta\ge0$, $\sin\theta$ starts repeating values after $\theta=\frac\pi2$, whereas $\cos\theta$ is one-to-one on $[0,\pi]$.

For $\sin3\theta=\frac12$, the first positive angles are
$$\theta=\frac\pi{18},\frac{5\pi}{18},\frac{13\pi}{18},\frac{17\pi}{18},\frac{25\pi}{18},\ldots$$
But $\sin\frac{13\pi}{18}=\sin\frac{5\pi}{18}$ and $\sin\frac{17\pi}{18}=\sin\frac\pi{18}$. Thus the first three angles give only two distinct values of $x$; continuing to $\frac{25\pi}{18}$ gives the third.

For $\cos3\theta=\frac12$, the first three nonnegative angles are $\frac\pi9$, $\frac{5\pi}9$ and $\frac{7\pi}9$. All lie in $[0,\pi]$, so their cosine values are distinct.
